analysis.title: GS - Lee - Macro cuRated - 23 Oct 2026
key_insights: Treasuries swung through the week of Oct 19-23: modest bear steepener Monday, twist-flattening Tuesday, bear-flattening Wednesday, a sharp belly-led rally Thursday, and a partial unwind Friday. Brent traded above $110 and closed Friday just shy of $117/bbl on intensifying Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure.

Thursday's rally came as the NDX fell roughly 3% on AI weakness (the GS AI basket is -23% since June) and 10y OAT-Bund widened about 15bp, pushing US 10y yields back below 5%. 2s rallied 19bp, 5s 20.7bp, 10s 19.3bp and 30s 15.2bp.
CTA positioning is at 87% of max short, with futures through all short-term buy triggers. The desk sees elevated short covering from here as momentum signals flip to buying.

Front-end policy pricing: the market goes into FOMC week with 2.7bp of hikes priced for the October meeting and 21.4bp cumulatively through year-end. Dec FOMC traded as low as 18bp on Thursday before settling near 22.5bp, and 1y1y fell about 24bp to roughly 4.60%.

FOMC is in blackout. The only scheduled Fed appearance next week is Chair Warsh's press conference on Wednesday. Thursday is the heaviest data day: advance Q3 GDP, September personal income, spending and PCE. Friday brings Q3 ECI and Chicago PMI. Coupon supply is 2s Monday, 5s Tuesday and 7s Thursday.

Rate vol trader (Mitchell Cornell, Volex Trading): vol ratcheted higher during the roughly 30bp rally in TY since the CPI-day cheaps, which is unusual because vol normally falls in a rally. Payer-long and receiver-short positions were hurt, client demand for receivers stayed strong, and thin liquidity amplified moves. Part of the vol move has since unwound with the selloff.

GS Econ estimates September core PCE at 3.1% y/y versus the Dallas Fed trimmed mean at 2.2%. Tariffs, the energy shock and AI-related price pressures and mismeasurement account for about 75% of the gap, and most of their sequential impact is judged to be behind us. GS keeps its view that inflation is not broadening and that the trimmed mean is a good guide.

Fed chatterbox: the consensus points to hiking every other meeting, which implies skipping October and hiking in December. Williams says one more hike may be appropriate, Logan says 50bp or more, and several participants see more than one additional hike. Almost all see the labor market as basically in balance.

October S&P Global PMIs: services 57.9 (-0.9pt, in line), manufacturing 56.0 (+0.1pt, highest since May 2022 if confirmed). Manufacturing input prices rose 8.4pt to 74.0 and output prices rose 7.1pt to 66.1. S&P says cost pressures are intensifying as oil reverberates through goods and services, and that firms find it easier to pass on costs.

GS estimates that a 15% AI productivity increase could temporarily displace about 9% of workers. Each 1% productivity gain raises unemployment by a temporary 0.3-0.4pp at peak. Displacement is driven more by job losses than weaker hiring, and it accelerates in cyclical slowdowns.

GS nowcasts central bank gold purchases at 79 tonnes in August versus a pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes, with China a large share. The 3-month seasonally adjusted pace is 85 tonnes a month. Foreign central bank gold at the NY Fed fell 40 tonnes in August while custodial holdings at the Bank of England rose 46 tonnes, which GS reads as a shift toward reserve security concerns.
French 10y yields topped 5% for the first time since 2002 on Wednesday, and 10y OAT-Bund widened about 15bp on Thursday.

macro_indicators.interpretation: GS estimate, ahead of Thursday's release. It is well above the Dallas Fed trimmed mean of 2.2%, supporting the Fed's view that further tightening is needed.

risk_factors: Further oil escalation from Houthi attacks and the Middle East could push yields higher.
AI-related equity weakness, including the highly levered AI names, could weigh on aggregate demand over the next 18 months to 2 years.
European sovereign stress, with French 10y above 5% and OAT-Bund widening.
Thin liquidity is amplifying duration and vol moves.
Persistent price pressures in PMIs, with intensifying supply chain bottlenecks.
AI-related labor disruption could amplify the business cycle in a slowdown.
vol_and_positioning: CTA positioning is at 87% of max short, with futures through all short-term buy triggers and short covering expected.
Rate vol was very bid Thursday and the surface aggressively flattened, with 1m10y vols +0.5bp/day (8th largest move in 252 trading days).
Rate vol ratcheted higher during a roughly 30bp TY rally since CPI-day cheaps, hurting payer-long and receiver-short positions.
Client demand for receivers remains strong as clients hedge lower-rate risks.
Hedge funds were better sellers of spreads Thursday and better receivers Friday. Real Money was two-way in swaps and receiving into Tuesday's rally.
geopolitical: Middle East: no resolution, with US-Iran deal headlines fading on doubts.
Reuters report that the US would order departures of some personnel from Gulf embassies, later clarified to apply only to some personnel in Saudi Arabia.
Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure intensified, pushing Brent close to $117/bbl.
French 10y yields topped 5% for the first time since 2002.

tension_points.bull_case: Risk-off and flight to quality drove belly-led rallies, with receiver demand strong and CTA short covering expected to extend the rally.
tension_points.bear_case: Oil near $117 and sticky price pressures, with PMI input prices at 74.0, kept rates cheap on Friday, and Fed officials see more hikes as likely.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A continued oil climb with equities stabilizing would reverse the flight-to-quality bid, as the Friday selloff showed.

tension_points.bull_case: Trimmed mean at 2.2% and fading one-off factors support the view that inflation is not broadening.
tension_points.bear_case: Core PCE at 3.1%, and Hammack and Goolsbee argue pressures are broad-based and persistent.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A rising share of upper-tail categories trimmed in consecutive months would signal a newly emerging persistent source of inflation.
